subject: physics
title: Ideal Gases and pV = nRT
welcome_lead: Push a piston, heat a balloon — and learn why pV = nRT works for every ideal gas.
meta_desc: A-Level Thermal Physics adventure on the ideal gas equation and gas laws.
final_note: Three variables linked by one equation: pressure, volume and absolute temperature.

concepts.def: Point particles with elastic collisions only.
Force per unit area: p = F/A, in pascals.
pV = constant at fixed T and n.

walkthroughs.body_html: pressure (Pa) × volume (m³) = moles × R × temperature (K). Always use Kelvin. Doubling temperature at fixed volume doubles pressure.
Fixed T: pV = constant (Boyle). Fixed p: V/T = constant (Charles). Fixed V: p/T = constant (Gay-Lussac). All come from pV = nRT.
Ideal gas assumes negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces and only elastic collisions. Real gases deviate at high pressure or low temperature.

mcqs.q: Which is true for an ideal gas at fixed n, T?
options: p V = constant
p / V = constant
p + V = constant
pV = T

mcqs.q: In the ideal gas equation pV = nRT, what must the temperature T be measured in?
options: Kelvin — the absolute temperature scale.
Either Celsius or Kelvin gives the same result.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Whatever units make the numbers work out neatly.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
options: Whatever units make the numbers work out neatly.
Heat is the energy transferred due to temperature difference; temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles.
Heat is measured in degrees Celsius and temperature in Joules.
Heat and temperature are the same thing — both measure how hot something is.

mcqs.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot water heat up faster than a wooden one?
options: Metals have higher thermal conductivity, so heat is transferred more rapidly through them.
Metal heats up faster because it has a lower specific heat capacity, requiring less energy per degree.
Heat is measured in degrees Celsius and temperature in Joules.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
